title: The Limit Laws
lead: Here limits are calculated by laws rather than read from tables and graphs: the limit laws for sums, products, quotients, powers and roots, the limits of polynomial and rational functions, the techniques for the indeterminate form 0/0 and the form K/0, and the squeeze theorem, which traps a function between two others and leads to the basic trigonometric limits.
objectives: Use the limit laws to evaluate the limit of a function.
Evaluate the limit of a function by factoring.
Use the limit laws to evaluate the limit of a polynomial or rational function.
Evaluate the limit of a function by factoring or by using conjugates.
Evaluate the limit of a function by using the squeeze theorem.
summary_html:
• The limit laws allow us to evaluate limits of functions without having to go through step-by-step processes each time.
  • For polynomials and rational functions, $\lim_{x\to a}\kf(x)=\kf(a).$
  • You can evaluate the limit of a function by factoring and canceling, by multiplying by a conjugate, or by simplifying a complex fraction.
  • The squeeze theorem allows you to find the limit of a function if the function is always greater than one function and less than another function with limits that are known.

$\lim_{x\to 0}(4{x}^{2}-2x+3)$

answer.solution: Use constant multiple law and difference law: $\lim_{x\to 0}(4{x}^{2}-2x+3)=4\lim_{x\to 0}{x}^{2}-2\lim_{x\to 0}x+\lim_{x\to 0}3=3$

For the following problems, evaluate the limit using the squeeze theorem. Use a calculator to graph the functions $f(x),g(x),$ and $h(x)$ when possible.

[T] True or False? If $2x-1\le g(x)\le {x}^{2}-2x+3,$ then $\lim_{x\to 2}g(x)=0.$

answer.solution: False. Both bounds are polynomials, so their limits at 2 come by direct substitution: $\lim_{x\to 2}(2x-1)=3$ and $\lim_{x\to 2}(x^{2}-2x+3)=4-4+3=3.$ The two bounds share the limit 3, so the squeeze theorem gives $\lim_{x\to 2}g(x)=3,$ not 0.

[T] In physics, the magnitude of an electric field generated by a point charge at a distance r in vacuum is governed by Coulomb’s law: $E(r)=\frac{q}{4\pi \varepsilon_{0}{r}^{2}},$ where E represents the magnitude of the electric field, q is the charge of the particle, r is the distance between the particle and where the strength of the field is measured, and $\frac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_{0}}$ is Coulomb’s constant: $8.988\;\times \;{10}^{9}\;\text{N}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{C}}^{2}.$ a. Use a graphing calculator to graph $E(r)$ given that the charge of the particle is $q={10}^{-10}.$ b. Evaluate $\lim_{r\to {0}^{+}}E(r).$ What is the physical meaning of this quantity? Is it physically relevant? Why are you evaluating from the right?

answer.solution: a. b. ∞. The magnitude of the electric field as you approach the particle q becomes infinite. It does not make physical sense to evaluate negative distance.

Evaluate the limit algebraically or explain why the limit does not exist.

$\lim_{x\to 4}\frac{4-x}{\sqrt{x}-2}$

Use the squeeze theorem to prove the limit.

$\lim_{x\to 0}x^{2}\cos(2\pi x)=0$

answer.solution: Since $-1\le\cos(2\pi x)\le 1,$ then $-x^{2}\le x^{2}\cos(2\pi x)\le x^{2}.$ Since $\lim_{x\to 0}x^{2}=0=\lim_{x\to 0}-x^{2},$ it follows that $\lim_{x\to 0}x^{2}\cos(2\pi x)=0.$

exercises.prompt:
Use the squeeze theorem to prove the limit.

$\lim_{x\to 0}x^{3}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{x}\right)=0$

answer.solution: For every $x\ne 0,$ $-1\le\sin(\pi/x)\le 1,$ and multiplying by $|x|^{3}\ge 0$ gives $-|x|^{3}\le |x|^{3}\sin(\pi/x)\le |x|^{3}.$ Since $x^{3}\sin(\pi/x)$ is $|x|^{3}\sin(\pi/x)$ or its negative, it lies between $-|x|^{3}$ and $|x|^{3}$ as well. By the power law and the limit of $|x|$, $\lim_{x\to 0}|x|^{3}=0=\lim_{x\to 0}(-|x|^{3}),$ so by the squeeze theorem $\lim_{x\to 0}x^{3}\sin(\pi/x)=0.$
